Abstract—Process-oriented programming is an approach to developing control software in which a
program is defined as a set of interacting processes. PoST is a process-oriented language, which is an
extension of the ST language from the IEC 61131-3 standard. In the field of control software develop-
ment, formal verification plays an important role due to the need to ensure high reliability of such soft-
ware. Deductive verification is a formal verification method in which a program and its requirements
are represented as logical formulas, and logical inference is used to prove that the program satisfies the
requirements. Control software often has temporal requirements. We formalize such requirements for
process-oriented programs as control loop invariants. However, control loop invariants that represent
requirements are not sufficient to prove the correctness of the program. Therefore, we add extra invari-
ants containing auxiliary information. This paper considers the problem of automating deductive ver-
ification of process-oriented programs. An approach is proposed in which temporal requirements are
specified using requirement patterns which are constructed from basic patterns. For each requirement
pattern, a corresponding extra invariant pattern and lemmas are defined. In this paper, the proposed
approach and schemes of basic and derived requirement patterns are described. The schemes of basic
extra invariant patterns, schemes of lemmas defined for basic patterns, and a set of basic patterns and
lemmas for them are considered. The scheme of derived extra invariant patterns and schemes of lem-
mas defined for derived patterns are defined. The algorithms for constructing derived extra invariant
patterns and lemmas for them, as well as methods for proving these lemmas are presented. The
schemes of proving verification conditions are considered. The proposed approach is demonstrated
with an example. The analysis of related works has also been carried out.
Keywords: deductive verification, temporal requirements, requirement pattern, loop invariant, control
software, process-oriented programming

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Process-oriented programming [1] is a promising methodology for developing control software. This paradigm describes a program as a collection of interacting processes. Each process behaves as an extended finite-state machine, defined by a set of named states that contain executable code. In addition to the active states explicitly defined in the program, each process includes two inactive states: STOP (indicating normal termination) and ERROR (signaling abnormal termination). Program execution proceeds cyclically. During each iteration of the control loop, all processes execute sequentially in their current states. The duration for which a process remains in a given state is governed by a timeout operator. Each process is associated with a timer that monitors this duration. The timer resets either when the process transitions to another state or through explicit program statements. Processes may launch or terminate other processes and query whether another process is currently active. Upon its first activation, a process transitions to the initial state specified in its definition. When the program starts, it activates only the first process, while all others remain inactive in the STOP state. The PoST language [2] extends the ST (Structured Text) language defined by the IEC 61131-3 standard [3] and provides specialized constructs for process-oriented programming. Each program or process may declare input variables (VAR_INPUT)— whose values the environment updates during each control cycle—output variables (VAR_OUTPUT)— which define control signals—and local variables (VAR). A process definition includes a sequence of state declarations. Given the stringent reliability requirements of control systems, formal verification becomes essential. Deductive verification [4] serves as one of the foundational methods in this domain. It formalizes the pro- gram’s specifications as logical formulas. From the program code and these formal specifications, the method generates verification conditions —logical expressions whose truth guarantees the program’s cor- rectness. Each loop in the program must include a loop invariant —a formula that holds upon entering the loop and remains valid after each iteration. Temporal properties form a significant class of requirements for control software. In [5], a method was proposed for specifying temporal requirements in process-oriented programs by encoding them as control loop invariants. This approach treats the program as a black box: requirements do not reference the inter- nal structure, such as process states, timer values, or local variables. However, such structural information is crucial when proving verification conditions. To address this, the control loop invariant is expressed as a conjunction of the formalized requirement and an extra invariant that contains structural information. Both types of invariants are formulated in the DV-TRL language [6], a typed first-order logic. DV-TRL builds on the update state data type, which captures complete histories of all program changes. Specialized functions over this type enable referencing variable values at specific time points, making it possible to express a wide range of temporal requirements. In deductive verification, only the generation of verification conditions can be fully automated. Syn- thesizing loop invariants and proving verification conditions are undecidable in the general case. None- theless, partial automation becomes feasible through targeted methods. One effective technique involves the use of patterns . In [7], the authors introduced a library of temporal requirement patterns written in DV-TRL. Each requirement pattern was paired with a corresponding extra invariant pattern, used to define the invariants needed for verification, and a set of lemmas necessary to prove the generated verification conditions. The authors also proposed extra invariant patterns that are independent of specific requirements. Together, these components made it possible to automate deduc- tive verification for a broad class of process-oriented programs. However, that approach required creating new requirement and extra invariant patterns for each novel type of requirement. Subsequent observations revealed that many previously developed patterns—and patterns capable of describing new requirement classes—can be systematically composed from a limited set of basic patterns . This paper introduces an enhanced pattern-based approach to automating deductive verification. Requirement patterns are now constructed by combining basic patterns according to predefined rules. Corresponding extra invariant patterns and lemmas, along with their proofs, can be automatically gen- erated. The structure of the paper is as follows. Section 1 presents the proposed verification framework and out- lines the general form (schemas) of basic and derived requirement patterns. Section 2 classifies basic require- ment patterns into future and past categories. For each, it introduces the corresponding extra invariant pat- terns and lemma schemas, including examples of practical pattern pairs and their associated lemmas. sections.text: Requirement-independent extra invariants capture relations among variable values, process states, and process timer values. These invariants take the form of quantifier-free formulas. One can extract them through static analysis of the process-oriented program. They are particularly useful in proving quantifier- free formulas in proving verification conditions using automated techniques. Because they are not tied to specific requirements, these invariants can assist in verifying a variety of properties. In contrast, requirement-dependent extra invariants describe supporting properties essential for prov- ing the satisfaction of specific requirements. These invariants typically relate variable values at different time points to process states, timer values, or other program variables evaluated at the point where the invariant is asserted. For each program, one can typically identify multiple requirement-independent extra invariants. However, each formal requirement is associated with a single requirement-dependent extra invariant. Both requirement patterns and requirement-dependent extra invariant patterns are classified as either basic or derived. A basic requirement pattern represents a predicate in the DV-TRL language that serves as a building block for constructing more complex, derived patterns. Each basic requirement pattern has a correspond- ing basic extra invariant pattern, which expresses the supporting properties necessary to prove instances of that basic requirement pattern. A derived requirement pattern defines some class of properties and serves as a parametric template for formalizing specific requirements. Its corresponding derived extra invariant pattern encodes the required extra invariants for such properties. In this context, the requirement-dependent extra invariant strength- ens the requirement itself—it asserts both the requirement and additional structural properties necessary for verification. Each basic (or derived) requirement pattern has an associated basic (or derived) extra invariant pattern and a related set of lemmas. The lemmas associated with a pair consisting of a basic requirement pattern and its corresponding extra invariant pattern enable one to reduce the proof of formulas involving these basic patterns to the proof of formulas that no longer contain them—except at the beginning of the loop iteration—and retain only their parameter values. These lemmas, in turn, support the proofs of lemmas for derived patterns that incorpo- rate such basic pattern instances. The lemmas associated with derived pattern pairs reduce the verification conditions and the lemmas for other derived patterns built upon them to simpler proof obligations. In many cases, applying simplified lem- mas yields quantifier-free formulas, which are amenable to automatic verification. This framework enables automatic generation of a derived extra invariant pattern and lemmas for a given derived requirement pattern, based solely on its parametric definition. Moreover, these lemmas can be proved automatically. To facilitate the verification process, we define proof scripts. These scripts, used in combination with the gen- erated lemmas, enable the automated discharge of verification conditions. sections.heading: 7. REVIEW OF RELATED WORK
sections.text: There exist many methods for searching for loop invariants. These include abstract interpretation [12], induction-iteration [13], methods based on templates [14], recurrence analysis [15], using failed proof attempts [16], strengthening of invariants on demand [17], dynamic analysis [18], and machine learning [19]. Abstract interpretation and methods based on templates are the most widespread in the field of static loop invariant synthesis. Methods for generating loop invariants based on templates are most successfully applied in the field of linear arithmetic [21]. In [14], a method is proposed for generating linear loop invariants based on tem- plates. The invariants have the form of linear inequalities. The authors generate constraints on the tem- plate parameters, which are coefficients in the inequality. These constraints guarantee that the invariant is true when the program enters the loop and after the loop iteration, if it is true before the iteration. To generate the constraints, Farkas’ lemma is used. The obtained constraints can be solved through quanti- fier elimination. However, since quantifier elimination is computationally expensive, the authors simplify the constraints using various methods. In our work, extra invariants are not linear inequalities that relate the values of program variables at one point, but formulas that relate the values of variables at different points in time and contain quantifiers by update states (in patterns). Currently, the values of pattern parameters are specified manually; we plan to explore the problem of constraint generation in future work. To search for parameter values in the template, one can use SMT solvers. In [22], an approach is pro- posed based on finding a satisfying assignment. The authors reduce the problem of finding template parameter values to a formula satisfiability problem, which allows them to use off-the-shelf solvers. The template parameter values are not constants, but expressions and predicates. To find such values, the authors formulate assumptions that reduce the task to searching for constants. To obtain these values, SMT solvers are used. In our work, pattern parameters are conditional expressions that include not only constants but also terms containing process timers. To reduce the problem of searching for such expres- sions to finding constants, we could consider instances of constraints for different paths in the program. STeP [23] uses two approaches to generate invariants: the bottom-up approach, where invariants are generated using static program analysis, and the top-down approach. In the top-down approach, invariant strengthening is used for unproven verification conditions. If some verification condition is not proven, the weakest precondition is computed relative to the invariant to be proved and the transition to which the verification condition corresponds. The strengthened invariant is a conjunction of the original invariant (which must be proven) and the computed weakest precondition. Both bottom-up and top-down invari- ants are used in our work. We could also use invariant strengthening. This approach must be used together with heuristics of replacing a constant with a term. However, it was noted that extra invariants that strengthen requirements satisfying the same pattern are similar and can also be described by a pattern. The article [24] is devoted to deductive verification of programs written in the LD language from the IEC 61131-3 standard. Temporal requirements for LD programs are specified using timing charts. The verification process uses the Why3 deductive verification system. The authors formalized LD instructions as Why3 functions. In this approach, an event and the subsequent stable state of the timing chart are mod- eled as a loop in Why3, where the loop body corresponds to a single iteration of the program’s control loop in LD. A loop condition represents a requirement that must be met by the input at the event moment and

We also noted that pattern for extra invariants can be defined to specify auxiliary properties and used instead of abstract interpretation. In [25], the authors propose a method of autoactive verification for automation of deductive verifica- tion. This approach requires users to provide additional guiding annotations such as assertions, ghost code, and lemma functions, to achieve a higher degree of proof automation. As a result, it allows the use of automatic solvers in cases where interactive proof tools have traditionally been used. The authors imple- ment autoactive verification for programs in C using the Frama-C framework. In our work, we do not use lemma functions. However, we can include formalized requirements as annotations in the program. For example, the loop invariant INV at the beginning of the loop can be expressed using the annotation ASSUME INV, while the invariant at the end of the loop can be expressed using ASSERT INV. Assertions can also be used to add auxiliary assertions at any point in the program. In [26], an approach is proposed that allows requirement specifications to be made reusable through object-oriented concepts. In this approach, in addition to declarative specifications for formulating requirements, a subset of the programming language is also used. For specifying temporal requirements, loops with invariants and ranking functions are used. The authors chose Eiffel as the programming lan- guage due to its features. Their approach is based on “specification drivers”, which are subprograms with contracts that define certain behavioral properties of their formal parameters through these contracts. The authors then describe templates for requirements using classes called seamless object-oriented require- ment templates. Each such class contains a specification driver and deferred features that corresponds to the pattern parameters. To define a requirement with such a template, a class is created representing the requirement and inherits from the class called a “seamless object-oriented requirement”, which rep- resents the requirement pattern and implements the required properties. In our work, we verify programs written in process-oriented languages, not object-oriented ones. We also define requirement patterns but do so in a first-order typed logic and do not use a programming language for requirement specification. We formulate temporal requirements as invariants of a control loop, which is a key concept of control soft- ware systems. In [27], a template-based method is combined with abstract interpretation and dynamic analysis to generate loop invariants. The template is a Boolean combination of linear inequalities. Every path in the program must satisfy the following condition: if the corresponding template instance is true at the begin- ning of the path, it must be true at the end. This condition is translated into a constraint. The constraints are nonlinear, and they are difficult to solve. Therefore, static and dynamic analysis are combined. Test scenarios for dynamic analysis are generated by other tools. In dynamic analysis, symbolic execution can be used. In dynamic analysis, variables in the program are replaced with values. This allows the generation of candidate invariants. Abstract interpretation is applied first; then dynamic analysis generates other invariants using a top-down method. In our work, we use only the template-based method and do not combine it with other methods. Similar to that work, we use both requirement-independent and require- ment-dependent invariants. sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: In this paper, we presented an approach to deductive verification of process-oriented programs in which requirements are specified using patterns based on basic requirement patterns. In this approach, a set of base patterns is defined. For each base requirement pattern, a corresponding base pattern of extra invariants and lemmas are also defined. The base requirement patterns can then be combined to define derived requirement patterns. For each derived requirement pattern, a corresponding pattern of extra invariants and lemmas are generated for proving verification conditions. The approach proposed in this paper makes it possible to automatically define patterns of extra invariants and lemmas needed to prove verification conditions for a given requirement and to prove these lemmas. By generalizing previously developed strategies for proving verification conditions so that they are parameter- ized by the corresponding lemma, we can automate proving verification conditions. Thus, the only task that remains to be fully automated is the determining values for parameters of extra invariant patterns.

sections.heading: PATTERN-BASED APPROACH TO THE AUTOMATION
sections.text: 1079 Currently, our library of requirement patterns includes 9 base patterns. Using them, we have defined 11 universal derived patterns that define classes , each of which includes at least two requirements, and 4 special derived patterns. These patterns allowed us to specify and verify all requirements from our col- lection, which contains 76 requirements from 12 control systems. However, the current pattern system does not yet allow us to define certain classes of requirements, such as those stating that a certain event should occur within a specified time interval after another event (requirements considered in [29]), or requirements that state a certain event must not occur until (before) a certain delay after another event. These types of timing constraints, such as “an event must occur k times” [30], are not yet covered by our system. We plan to extend our pattern system to include these classes of requirements. In the future, we plan to develop tools for generating derived patterns of extra invariants and lemmas, as well as scripts for proving verification conditions. We also plan to develop a heuristic algorithm for find- ing values of parameters for patterns of extra invariants.
